intro: Hands-on Linux Essentials labs graded in your browser: a simulated Ubuntu terminal for files, text processing, permissions, archives and processes, plus drills on the file system layout, licenses and commands.

labs.title: Organize files from the command line
labs.summary: Move around the file system, make directories, copy, move, rename and delete files, and find a hidden file.
labs.scenario:
Your ~/downloads folder is a mess. Tidy it up from the terminal:

  • Create ~/projects/2026/reports in one command
  • Copy both report-q1.txt and report-q2.txt into it (keep the originals)
  • Create ~/pictures and move photo.jpg there, renamed to vacation.jpg
  • Delete the old installer old-installer.deb
  • There's also a hidden file in ~/downloads. Find it and read the guest Wi-Fi code inside

tasks.text: Both reports are copied into it, and the originals are still in ~/downloads
What is the guest Wi-Fi code?

hints: cd ~/downloads then ls -la. Names that start with a dot are hidden.
mkdir -p creates every missing directory in the path.
cp SOURCE... DEST/ copies; mv OLD NEW moves and renames in one step.
labs.solution:
mkdir -p ~/projects/2026/reports
cp ~/downloads/report-q1.txt ~/downloads/report-q2.txt ~/projects/2026/reports/
mkdir ~/pictures
mv ~/downloads/photo.jpg ~/pictures/vacation.jpg
rm ~/downloads/old-installer.deb
ls -la ~/downloads
cat ~/downloads/.wifi-notes
labs.review: Absolute paths start at /; relative paths start from where you are; ~ is your home. cp leaves the original, mv doesn't, and rm has no recycle bin.

labs.title: Search and count with pipes
labs.summary: Use grep, wc, cut, sort, uniq and redirection to answer questions about log files and save the results.
labs.scenario:
The order app on ubuntu01 had a bad morning. Its logs are in /var/log/app/: app.log and access.log. Use pipes to answer the team's questions, and save two results to files in your home directory:

  • ~/errors.txt: every ERROR line from app.log, and nothing else
  • ~/users.txt: the account names from /etc/passwd, sorted alphabetically, one per line

content: 2026-10-29 08:09:57 ERROR user=jsmith payment gateway timeout order=1009
2026-10-29 08:11:23 ERROR user=priya payment gateway timeout order=1011
2026-10-29 08:22:46 ERROR user=maria payment gateway timeout order=1022
2026-10-29 08:24:12 ERROR user=jsmith payment gateway timeout order=1024
2026-10-29 08:35:35 ERROR user=alex payment gateway timeout order=1035
2026-10-29 08:37:01 ERROR user=maria payment gateway timeout order=1037

tasks.text: How many ERROR lines are in app.log?
Which IP address made the most requests in access.log?

check.equals:
2026-10-29 08:09:57 ERROR user=jsmith payment gateway timeout order=1009
2026-10-29 08:11:23 ERROR user=priya payment gateway timeout order=1011
2026-10-29 08:22:46 ERROR user=maria payment gateway timeout order=1022
2026-10-29 08:24:12 ERROR user=jsmith payment gateway timeout order=1024
2026-10-29 08:35:35 ERROR user=alex payment gateway timeout order=1035
2026-10-29 08:37:01 ERROR user=maria payment gateway timeout order=1037

tasks.text: Save the sorted account names to ~/users.txt

hints: grep ERROR FILE | wc -l counts matching lines (or use grep -c).
The IP is the first field: cut -d" " -f1 access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head.
> saves output to a file. In /etc/passwd fields are separated by colons: cut -d: -f1.
labs.solution:
cd /var/log/app
grep -c ERROR app.log
cut -d" " -f1 access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3
grep ERROR app.log > ~/errors.txt
cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd | sort > ~/users.txt
labs.review: Small tools joined with pipes answer most log questions: filter (grep), cut out a field (cut, awk), sort, count duplicates (uniq -c), and keep the top lines (head).

labs.title: Users, groups and permissions
labs.summary: Create a group, add a user to it, build a shared directory, and set file permissions with chmod.
labs.scenario:
Marketing needs a shared folder on ubuntu01, and two of your own files need tighter permissions.

  • Create the group marketing and add the existing user maria to it (she keeps her other groups)
  • Create /srv/marketing, owned by root with group marketing; the owner and group get full access and others get nothing
  • ~/backup.sh: you can read, write and run it; the group can read it; others get nothing
  • ~/private.txt: only you can read and write it
hints: Group and user changes need root: sudo groupadd marketing, then sudo usermod -aG marketing maria. Without -a, usermod replaces her groups.
r=4, w=2, x=1. Add them per position: owner, group, others.
sudo chown root:marketing /srv/marketing sets owner and group together.
labs.solution:
sudo groupadd marketing
sudo usermod -aG marketing maria
id maria
sudo mkdir /srv/marketing
sudo chown root:marketing /srv/marketing
sudo chmod 770 /srv/marketing
chmod 740 ~/backup.sh
chmod 600 ~/private.txt
ls -l ~ /srv
labs.review: Permissions are three sets (owner, group, others) of read, write and execute. Groups let several users share files without opening them to everyone.

labs.title: Back up and restore with tar
labs.summary: Create a compressed tar archive, list what's inside, and restore it to a different folder.
labs.scenario:
Before a laptop upgrade, back up ~/projects and test the restore:

  • Create ~/backup/projects.tar.gz, a gzip-compressed archive of ~/projects
  • List the archive's contents without extracting it
  • Extract it into /tmp/restore and check that index.html came back

tasks.text: ~/backup/projects.tar.gz is a gzip archive containing the website

hints: c = create, t = list, x = extract, z = gzip, f = the archive file name (put f last).
Run tar from your home directory so the paths inside the archive are relative: cd ~.
-C DIR extracts into another directory, which must exist first.
labs.solution:
cd ~
mkdir backup
tar -czf backup/projects.tar.gz projects
tar -tzf backup/projects.tar.gz
mkdir /tmp/restore
tar -xzf backup/projects.tar.gz -C /tmp/restore
ls /tmp/restore/projects/website
labs.review: tar bundles files; gzip (-z), bzip2 (-j) or xz (-J) compress the bundle. Always test a restore: a backup you can't restore isn't a backup.

labs.title: Processes, disk space and network info
labs.summary: Find and stop a runaway process, and look up who runs a process, how full the disk is and the server's IP address.
labs.scenario: Users say ubuntu01 is slow. Something you started earlier is using all the CPU. Find it and stop it, then gather a few facts for the help desk ticket.

tasks.text: Look at the running processes with ps or top
Stop the process that's using all the CPU
How full is the root (/) file system?
What is the server's IPv4 address?

hints: ps aux shows every process with its user and CPU use; top sorts by CPU.
kill PID stops a process you own.
df -h shows disk use; ip addr shows addresses.
labs.review: Every process has an ID and an owner. You can stop your own processes; stopping other users' processes needs root. df reports space per file system and ip addr shows interface addresses.

labs.title: Linux and open source essentials
labs.summary: Match the main directories of the file system hierarchy, open source licenses, and common commands to what they do.
labs.scenario: You're preparing a one-page cheat sheet for new team members.

activities.title: Where things live
activities.prompt: Match each directory to what it holds.

items.text: Temporary files that can be deleted

activities.title: Licenses
activities.prompt: Match each license to its description.

items.text: Copyleft: modified versions you distribute must stay open
Short permissive license; keep the notice and do almost anything
Permissive, with an explicit patent grant
Often used for documents, images and other non-software works

activities.title: Commands
activities.prompt: Match each command to its job.

items.text: Show the manual for a command

hints: /var holds data that changes while the system runs, including logs.
labs.review: The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard keeps every distribution's layout familiar, and knowing licenses tells you what you may do with code you find.

labs.title: Break it, then fix it: 'Permission denied' on your own file
labs.summary: Remove all permissions from a report, see the error, read the mode with ls -l and restore sensible permissions.
labs.scenario:
You own ~/reports/q3.txt. Practice the failure on purpose:

  1. Read it: cat ~/reports/q3.txt
  2. Break it: chmod 000 ~/reports/q3.txt
  3. Try to read it again and note the message
  4. Look at the permissions with ls -l ~/reports
  5. Fix it: owner read and write, group read, others nothing

tasks.text: Read the file while it still works
Fix it: mode 640, still owned by student
Verify you can read it again

questions.prompt: You own the file but cat says 'Permission denied'. Why?
options: The mode removed read permission for everyone, including the owner
The file is in the wrong directory
You need to be root to read any file

hints: chmod 640 FILE = owner rw-, group r--, others ---.
labs.solution:
cat ~/reports/q3.txt
chmod 000 ~/reports/q3.txt
cat ~/reports/q3.txt     # Permission denied
ls -l ~/reports
chmod 640 ~/reports/q3.txt
cat ~/reports/q3.txt
labs.review: Permissions apply to the owner too: with mode 000 nobody can read the file, even its owner. ls -l shows the nine permission bits that explain the error.
